papers.abstract: Abstract We study worker noncompete clauses in a large field experiment with two finance firms. papers.title: International Arbitrage Premia
papers.abstract: Abstract We introduce the nonlinear arbitrage correction (NAC), the residual that renders a linear benchmark model arbitrage-free while preserving the law of one price. The price of NAC captures the marginal Sharpe ratio increase consistent with no-arbitrage and upper-bounds the constrained Hansen–Jagannathan distance. Using four decades of international equity, currency, and factor returns, NAC is strongly countercyclical, peaking during crises when linear models turn negative. papers.title: Size-Based Regulation and Bank Fragility: Evidence from the Wells Fargo Asset Cap
papers.abstract: Abstract We argue that heightened regulation on large banks contributed to the rise in fragility of smaller banks revealed by the 2023 regional bank crisis. In 2018, regulators restricted Wells Fargo, the third largest U.S. bank, from growing its total assets. We estimate this asset cap led Wells Fargo to give up deposits amounting to 2.2% of aggregate bank deposits. These deposits, primarily uninsured, were reallocated to banks geographically proximate to Wells Fargo, including smaller, less regulated banks. DP22073 Losing grip? The Quantity Theory of Money under Currency Competition
authors: Jasmina Arifovic, Isabelle Salle, Linda Schilling
papers.abstract: This study examines monetary policy under competition between a centrally managed currency (the “Dollar”) and a fixed-supply alternative (the “Peso”). Theory and laboratory evidence reveal two equilibrium types. In the pass-through equilibrium, Dollar inflation is high and trade effects are limited. In the substitution equilibrium, Dollar dominance rises and velocity falls, muting Dollar inflation while generating inflation spillovers to Peso despite its fixed supply. papers.title: When Should We (Not) Interpret Linear IV Estimands as LATE?
papers.abstract: Abstract In this paper I revisit the interpretation of the linear instrumental variables (IV) estimand as a weighted average of conditional local average treatment effects (LATEs). I focus on a situation in which additional covariates are required for identification while the reduced-form and first-stage regressions may be misspecified due to an implicit homogeneity restriction on the effects of the instrument. papers.title: Robust Aggregation of Correlated Information
papers.abstract: Abstract Decisions are typically made by drawing on multiple sources of information, yet the correlation among these sources is often hard to assess. We study robustly optimal strategies—those that maximize the worst-case payoff guarantee across all correlation structures. With two states and two actions, the robustly optimal strategy is strikingly simple: use only the best information source and ignore the rest. papers.title: Share Issues vs. Share Repurchases
papers.abstract: Almost all firms repurchase shares through open-market repurchase programs. In contrast, issue methods are more diverse; at-the-market offerings, analogous to open-market repurchases, and seasoned equity offerings, analogous to rarely used tender-offer repurchases, are both used by significant fractions of firms. Furthermore, average seasoned equity offerings are larger than at-the-market offerings. papers.title: DP22072 Dynamic Test Design
papers.abstract: We study dynamic test design under the threat of manipulation. At each instant, a principal who cannot commit to future actions chooses whether to hire an agent, fire him, or continue costly probation by designing a test. The test provides information about the agent’s persistent type, which is either good or bad. After observing the test choice, the bad type can exert costly effort to manipulate the evidence and mimic the good type. papers.title: DP22071 Entry, Exit, and Technological Progress in Markov-Perfect Duopoly
authors: Jaap Abbring, Jeffrey Campbell, Nan Yang
papers.abstract: This paper establishes the existence and essential uniqueness of an intuitively refined Markov-perfect equilibrium in a duopoly game with sunk costs, barriers to entry, firm-specific technological progress, and irreversible exit. We develop an algorithm that quickly computes the equilibrium by solving for fixed points of a finite sequence of auxiliary contraction mappings, which we label Fake Backward Induction. authors: Yao Chen, Ricardo Duque Gabriel, Mathias Klein, Ana Sofia Pessoa

We document this using two innovations. papers.title: DP22065 Does Easy Money Win Elections?
authors: Yao Chen, Florian van Genderen, Felix Ward
papers.abstract: Governments press central banks for lower interest rates on the premise that easy money wins elections. We test this premise for 385 elections in 18 countries, 1900–2020, using exogenous interest rate changes. We find no evidence that monetary easing helps incumbents. At the point estimate, a typical easing leaves the incumbent’s vote share unchanged; the one-sided 95 percent confidence bound on the gain is 0.90 percentage points. papers.title: DP22068 Inside Central Bankers’ Calendars: How Do Fed Chairs Allocate Their Time?
papers.abstract: How leaders allocate their limited time and attention is an important question in economics. This paper constructs and analyzes a novel data set covering the daily calendars of three Federal Reserve Chairs, Ben Bernanke, Janet Yellen, and Jerome Powell, containing more than 20,000 calendar entries. We document several patterns. First, all Fed Chairs spend more than 30% of their documented meetings with Fed staff, highlighting the crucial role of economists in the Fed's decision process. papers.title: DP22067 Competitive Search for Bundles
papers.abstract: How does buyers’ search for bundles generate sorting among heterogeneous sellers? We study competitive search in which buyers assemble bundles through separate transactions, where prices direct search and determine congestion. With two seller types, buyers choose only same-type bundles below a single threshold in cross-type value and cross-type bundles above it. The threshold lies strictly between geometric and arithmetic means of same-type values, so search produces cross-type matching even when types are complements. papers.title: DP22069 Foreign Ownership and Occupational Safety: Evidence from France
authors: Beata Javorcik, Alessia Lo Turco, Daniela Maggioni, Gianluca Santoni
papers.abstract: This paper examines whether and how foreign acquisitions improve occupational safety. Using linked administrative data on French manufacturing plants over 2003–2017 and event studies on a matched sample, we find that foreign acquisitions reduce accident rates and workdays lost. Safety gains coincide with expanded managerial hierarchies, greater technical-manager presence, foreign manager hiring, and worker training. papers.title: DP22062 The Depositary of Last Resort
papers.abstract: What are the consequences of making central bank deposits accessible to actors beyond the banking sector? We collect novel micro data on deposit accounts historically held with the Bank of England by individuals and firms other than banks to study their role in the financial panic of 1866. We document that the use of deposit accounts at the central bank soared during the crisis, while commercial banks permanently lost funding. authors: Laura Alfaro, Maggie Chen, Beata Javorcik
papers.abstract: Multinational corporations (MNCs) create and transfer knowledge across countries. Economists have focused on how these flows affect productivity and growth. Policymakers, however, increasingly emphasize a geopolitical externality: knowledge that strengthens a rival state's strategic capabilities imposes on the home country costs the transferring firm does not internalize. papers.title: DP22066 Fiscal-Monetary Interactions: The Role of Debt Maturity
authors: Luca Bettarelli, Davide Furceri, Francesco Frangiamore, Anh Dinh Minh Nguyen, Francesco Scianna
papers.abstract: This paper examines how the maturity structure of sovereign debt shapes fiscal–monetary interactions in the United States. Using exogenous monetary policy shocks and nonlinear local projections, we show that debt maturity influences both the fiscal consequences of monetary tightening and its macroeconomic transmission. papers.title: DP22061 Importers, Market Power and Optimal Tariffs
authors: Jonathan Becker, Corina Boar, Virgiliu Midrigan
papers.abstract: Importers are few and large, have higher labor productivity and pass through cost changes to prices incompletely. We study optimal tariffs in a model consistent with these facts. Firms pay a fixed cost to import and charge markups that increase with size. Market power implies that importers are too few and too small relative to the efficient allocations. Tariffs amplify this distortion. papers.title: DP22063 Committee Deliberation and Gender Differences in Influence
papers.abstract: This paper provides empirical evidence on the aggregation of information in hiring committees. We use data from the hiring process of a large company in which committee members first conduct independent one-on-one interviews and then deliberate to reach a collective hiring decision. Results show that the mapping of committee members' initial assessments to final decisions is not deterministic, leaving scope for deliberation and individual influence. Committee decisions are systematically less aligned with recommendations made by women than with those made by men, despite similar qualifications

papers.title: How Private Equity Fuels Nonbank Lending
papers.abstract: Abstract We demonstrate how private equity (PE) promotes nonbank lending by substituting for bank monitoring. Relative to non-PE-backed loans, PE-backed loans exhibit lower bank monitoring, smaller loan shares retained by lead banks, and larger shares held by nonbanks. The substitution is strongest when sponsors have greater incentives to engage with portfolio firms, is not associated with weaker loan performance, and persists during borrower distress. papers.title: Optimal Information and Security Design
papers.abstract: Abstract An asset owner designs an asset-backed security and a signal about its value. After experiencing a liquidity shock and privately observing the signal, he sells the security to imperfectly competitive buyers. With flexible information design, the security’s informational sensitivity is a blessing, not a curse. Among double-monotone securities, the issuer prefers to sell the asset in combination with an appropriate signal rather than design more complex securities. papers.title: Insurance and Assurance: Government Interventions and Depositor Behavior in Crisis
papers.abstract: Abstract We examine how different forms of government intervention - explicit deposit insurance, implicit guarantees from nationalization, and assurance effects from re-privatization - shape depositor behavior during a banking crisis. Using proprietary monthly account-level data, we show that depositors respond to formal insurance limits even in an environment of broad state support, but adjust only partially. papers.title: Disagreement and Bond PEAD
papers.abstract: This paper documents post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) in corporate bond prices using transaction data. We find a counterintuitive relationship between the drift and trading volume: PEAD is more pronounced for more heavily traded bonds than for less frequently traded bonds. Across markets, PEAD is observed for credit default swaps but not for stocks. We explain these findings using a unified model that incorporates both debt and equity trading, where investors possess private information about the underlying firm’s cash flows and may hold differing opinions. papers.title: Conditional and Lenient Drug Approvals
papers.abstract: Firms are often allowed to sell new drugs based on preliminary efficacy evidence, with final approval contingent on confirmatory testing. We characterize optimal approval policies for a government agency that maximizes consumer welfare while considering the firm’s incentives. We assume that firms have private information about testing costs and the government’s payoff depends on the drug’s expected efficacy. papers.title: DP22058 The Great Game: A Model of Geoeconomic Competition
authors: Christopher Clayton, Matteo Maggiori, Jesse Schreger
papers.abstract: We build a model of two hegemons that have valuable trading relationships with each other and at the same time compete in exerting geoeconomic power over countries in the rest of the world. When the hegemons trade with each other, their optimal policy is shaped both by classic economic considerations - the profitability of that specific trade - and by geoeconomic competition - how the trade affects the power of each hegemon vis-a-vis the rest of the world. papers.title: DP22060 Artificial Intelligence and Climate Change: Balancing Innovation and Sustainability
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important factor in the climate transition. AI can improve energy efficiency, optimise resource use, accelerate climate innovation and strengthen climate forecasting, adaptation and risk management. At the same time, the development and deployment of AI require substantial computational resources, increasing electricity demand and, depending on the carbon intensity and timing of electricity use, associated emissions. papers.title: DP22059 Transition Risk in Emerging Economies
authors: Stefano Carattini, Giseong Kim, Givi Melkadze, Aude Pommeret
papers.abstract: Many emerging economies tend to rely considerably on carbon-intensive sectors, exposing themselves to potential transition risk. This paper quantifies the impact of this risk and the role of various policies and policy designs in mitigating it. It does so with a two-country two-sector environmental dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model, where each “country” represents a bloc of advanced or emerging economies, respectively. papers.title: DP22055 Do Equity Markets Spur Corporate Detox?
authors: Ali Ataullah, Hang Le, Alexander F. Wagner
papers.abstract: This paper provides archival and experimental evidence that equity market feedback influences firms' environmental behavior. Following the publication of U.S. Reports on Carcinogens, firms using newly identified carcinogens that experience particularly negative stock-price reactions reduce toxic waste more, especially when their worker exposure is high. Cross-sectional tests show stronger effects where market signals are likely to be more informative, and peer-firm evidence suggests that firms also learn from affected firms' stock-price reactions. papers.title: DP22054 The Foreign Currency Risk of International Remittances
papers.abstract: We study the role of foreign currency risk in remittance markets, and its consequences for fees and market structure. Because operators quote fees before settling transfers, exchange rate risk that is costly to hedge in thin currency markets enters their marginal cost, keeping fees high even in competitive corridors. We test this using 34,680 cash-to-cash products across 339 corridors between 2011 and 2024. papers.title: DP22053 When Cash Flows Turn Negative: Liquidity-Driven Selling by Pension Funds
authors: Aleksandar Andonov, Kristy Jansen, Joshua Rauh
papers.abstract: Pension funds are long-horizon investors with predictable liability structures. As such, they are often perceived as investors who can provide liquidity and stabilize markets. However, pension funds increasingly face negative operating cash flows as benefit payments exceed contributions. Using aggregate data on U.S. public pension funds combined with granular holdings obtained through public records requests, we document three findings that challenge the conventional view of pension funds as stabilizing investors. papers.title: DP22057 Measuring Common Ownership: An Axiomatic Approach
papers.abstract: This paper proposes three basic axioms for measuring common ownership based purely on the ownership distributions: symmetry, normalization, and orthogonality. Combining a fourth, structural axiom with normalization yields a characterization of cosine similarity as the only commonality measure that satisfies all axioms. The paper also discusses how the basic axioms relate to measures of common ownership used in empirical research.

papers.title: DP22051 Who Controls the Defence Industry?
authors: Marco Becht, Juan Mejino-López, Guntram B. Wolff
papers.abstract: Defence markets exhibit extreme asset specificity and bilateral monopoly. Transaction-cost economics predicts state ownership or control in such circumstances. This paper examines what governments actually do. Ownership alone does not determine control. A state with zero equity can still have influence through governance provisions and legal tools. Using large language model extraction from annual reports, supplemented by hand-coding, we compile a leximetric dataset on corporate governance and state control for 107 of the world's largest defence companies, drawn from the SIPRI Top 100 for 2022

papers.title: DP22052 The Price of Position: Spatial Equilibrium in the Geostationary Arc
papers.abstract: How costly is uniform congestion pricing when locations differ in value? I study the geostationary orbit, where satellites serve different markets from recorded positions and supported $77 billion in satellite television revenues in 2023. I estimate a spatial model of commercial entry in which efficient charges rise with demand. In the baseline estimates, the optimal uniform charge captures 66 percent of the attainable welfare gain, or 79 percent when income replaces population as the demand measure. papers.title: DP22050 Monetary Policy Uncertainty and Bank Credit Allocation
authors: Fatih Altunok, Yavuz Arslan, Steven Ongena
papers.abstract: We analyze how monetary policy uncertainty (MPU) affects bank credit allocation. First, we develop a theoretical model in which MPU consumes banks’ risk-bearing capacity. Higher MPU therefore curbs risky lending, most strongly at less capitalized banks. Second, we test this prediction across U.S. credit markets using FOMC-announcement changes in option implied rate uncertainty, controlling for the monetary policy stance. papers.title: DP22056 Political Ideology and Durable Spending
authors: Yongqiang Chu, Francesco D'Acunto, Janet Geo, Roman Wang, Yichen Wang
papers.abstract: Research in psychology suggests that conservatives should focus more on the investment value of durables, whereas liberals on consumption value. We test this hypothesis by examining the differential housing transaction motives of conservative and liberal households. Similar to other durable goods, housing assets embody both consumption and investment values and represent the largest assets of U.S. households. papers.title: DP22049 Geopolitics and Rule-Based Trade
papers.abstract: We analyze the stability of rule-based trade when trading partners differ in their geopolitical objectives. We show that asymmetric gains from trade and geopolitical benefits can generate asymmetric equilibria in which one country infringes and the other tolerates the violation even though there is repeated trade. papers.title: DP22045 The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
authors: David Deming, Raffaella Sadun, Christopher Stanton
papers.abstract: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development. papers.abstract: When technical progress arises from the decreasing cost of machines performing tasks that are highly substitutable with some type of labor, perfect competition may exacerbate wage inequality and concentrate the benefits of economic growth on the workers who are performing less routine tasks. authors: Kirill Borusyak, Rafael Dix-Carneiro, Brian Kovak
papers.abstract: A commonly used migration regression relates population changes to local labor demand shocks, often yielding small or statistically insignificant coefficients despite sizable effects on labor market outcomes. We argue that such findings need not imply that mobility is unresponsive to local economic conditions. authors: Ernest Liu, Stephen Redding, Bennett Smith-Worthington, David Yang
papers.abstract: We develop a tractable framework for analyzing geopolitics as a network of coordination and strategic influence. Countries choose geopolitical actions that trade off domestic interests against incentives to align with connected countries. They can exert costly bilateral influence to affect one another's actions. We characterize equilibrium actions and bilateral influence in closed form. Cross-country differences in domestic interests decompose into latent geopolitical cleavages, each of which the network transmits into geopolitical actions independently of the others. The cross-country covaria

papers.title: Measuring Measurement Error
papers.abstract: Abstract We collect 2,848 instrumental variable (IV) regressions from 391 papers published in top economics and finance journals and show that estimated IV coefficients are often much larger than their OLS counterparts, even when theory suggests they should be smaller. We derive meta-regression estimators that distinguish measurement error bias from omitted variable bias and simultaneity bias; applying our estimators to a set of 1,040 comparable regressions from 139 papers, we find that measurement error shrinks reported coefficients by about two to four times. Measurement error remains quanti

papers.title: Competition and Diversity in Generative AI
papers.abstract: Recent evidence, both in the laboratory and in the wild, suggests that the use of generative artificial intelligence reduces the diversity of content produced. As generative AI penetrates more markets and reaches widespread adoption, should we still expect to see content homogenization? Our work begins with a simple observation: content producers do not act in isolation. Instead, they compete with one another (e.g., for customers or attention). We explore the impact competition has on both content diversity and overall social welfare when producers use generative AI. Through a formal game-theo

papers.title: The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through
papers.abstract: Behavioral interventions often focus on reducing friction to encourage behavior change. In contrast, we provide evidence that adding initial friction to a sign-up process can increase follow-through behavior. In a field experiment with a state department of transportation ([Formula: see text]), we test whether adding modest friction during sign-up for a carpool platform increases usage. Although a more effortful sign-up process leads to 25% fewer sign-ups, overall usage increases. Importantly, these results were only partly explained by selection: Using an intent-to-treat analysis, participant

papers.title: DP22041 Non-Academic Criteria for Admission to Israeli Medical Schools: Recommendations for Change
papers.abstract: Three of the top medical schools in Israel (Hebrew University, Tel Aviv University, and the Technion) use the so-called "MOR—MIRKAM" exam as the non-academic criterion in their medical school admissions. Candidates who clear the demanding cognitive thresholds at these three universities are then evaluated at a second stage by one of two assessment centers (MOR or MIRKAM) administered by the National Institute for Testing and Evaluation (NITE). In the final admission score, the Hebrew University places a 60% weight on the MOR—MIRKAM exam and 40% on the cognitive scores, while Tel Aviv Universit

papers.title: DP22042 The Labor Market Effects of GLP-1s: Evidence from Weight Management and Diabetes Cohorts
authors: Christian Aleman, Fane Groes, Veda Narasimhan, Raül Santaeulàlia-Llopis, Tanya Surovtseva
papers.abstract: Using population-wide administrative microdata from Denmark, we provide the first comprehensive empirical evaluation contrasting the causal labor market effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists across their dual therapeutic tracks: a subsidized diabetic cohort (Ozempic) subject to public reimbursement, and a weight-management cohort (Wegovy) paying entirely out-of-pocket. Exploiting variation in individual prescription timing among eventual users, and validated by a battery of robustness checks leveraging treatment dropouts, alternative insulin baselines, and matched stacked designs, we find robust

papers.title: DP22043 Tax Productivity and Economic Development: A Quantitative Macroeconomic Analysis
authors: Radhika Goyal, Anders Jensen, David Lagakos, Abdoulaye Ndiaye, Yuntian Zhao
papers.abstract: This paper examines the role of government capacity to collect taxes in driving economic development. We first draw on a new macro-historical database to document that tax collections relative to tax administration expenditures rise sharply with GDP per capita. We then interpret this finding in a neoclassical growth model with a tax administration sector in which labor inputs are required to raise tax revenues. Countries differ in their levels of tax productivity, capturing how effectively labor is used to raise taxes, as well as their levels of productivity in creating consumption and investm

papers.title: DP22044 Competitive Centrality: Equilibrium and Comparative Statics in Networks
authors: Jian Li, Yves Zenou, Junjie Zhou
papers.abstract: We study equilibrium behavior and the propagation of local shocks in networked competition. We introduce competitive centrality, a nonlinear centrality measure that is uniquely determined by network primitives and provides a sufficient statistic for equilibrium behavior. It determines players’ effort allocations and winning probabilities in each bilateral competition. We then use competitive centrality to derive exact expressions for equilibrium responses to local shocks and characterize their signs. Local shocks propagate along network paths according to players’ relative competitive position

papers.title: DP22040 Improved Optimal Investment and Consumption Strategies under Inflation Risk with Stochastic Volatility
authors: Wouter Honig, Michel Vellekoop, Roel Beetsma, Bart Diris
papers.abstract: This paper develops and calibrates a financial market model that incorporates stochastic volatility in inflation, interest rate and equity dynamics. Traditional models typically assume constant inflation volatility, which limits investors’ responsiveness to economic shifts as a result of geopolitical tensions and events such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Our multidimensional affine model structure therefore extends the classical Brennan and Xia (2002) framework with a macroeconomic stochastic variance component that allows the model to capture the interdependence of asset price returns and inflati

papers.title: Closing Ranks: Organized Labor and Immigration
A Theory of Economic Coercion and Fragmentation
Shipment Monitoring, Allocation, and the Impact on Food Waste
papers.abstract: Often advocated for the potential to reduce waste in fresh produce supply chains, sensor technologies enable firms to monitor the condition of each product unit and allocate them to markets at different transportation distances, thereby matching units with shorter shelf lives with closer markets. In this paper, we consider a firm purchasing and transporting a fresh produce product for sale in two destination markets. Postharvest processes cause a proportion of the product to be in risky condition, potentially becoming unsalable (“spoiled”) due to shelf-life deterioration during transportation.

papers.title: Retail on Wheels: A Time-Sensitive Traveling Salesman Problem
papers.abstract: Rapid advancement in self-driving technology has brought mobile retail into the spotlight. Motivated by its potential, we present a model, theory, and insights into the operations of mobile retail, where a fleet of wheeled stores traverses a service region, selectively seeks locations in which to perch, and fulfills local customer demand. The goal of retailers is to strike a balance between perching and migrating to maximize total revenue. To dispatch such stores, retailers need to consider the following time-sensitive factors: (i) how busy the service is, (ii) how soon customers will arrive,

papers.title: Externalities of Responsible Investments
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a model to study the efficiency of socially responsible investing (SRI) as a mechanism to control firms' externalities. When SRI is not too popular, responsible investors favor strategies that lead to a concentration of SRI in a subset of firms in the economy. This concentration can mitigate coordination issues in adopting green technologies, but it can also crowd out the green investments of excluded firms and increase the price of green products. In equilibrium, responsible investors continue to favor concentration even as SRI becomes more popular, and concentrate the mos

papers.title: Systemically Important Banks and Loan Performance: Evidence from India
papers.abstract: We examine whether designating banks as systemically important affects loan performance in an emerging-market setting where such banks are large domestic institutions and market imperfections make monitoring crucial for loan performance. Using loan-level data and the staggered designation of banks as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (DSIBs) in India, we find that loan performance deteriorates following DSIB designation. The evidence points to bank-level moral hazard as the underlying mechanism: DSIBs reduce postorigination monitoring and weaken loan recovery efforts. Borrowers respond acc

papers.title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
papers.abstract: We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level d

papers.title: Why Do We Discriminate? Directional Beliefs and Biased Information Processing
papers.abstract: Identifying the cause of discrimination is crucial to designing effective policies and to understanding discrimination dynamics. This paper provides a potential link between existing models of taste-based and statistical discrimination by studying directional belief formation through biased information search and processing. By selectively acquiring and processing information, individuals form directional beliefs and consequently discriminate based on these beliefs. Through a series of experiments in which individuals endogenously acquire and process various signals, I document discrimination

papers.title: DP22039 Multimarket Contact and the Southwest Effect: Twenty-Five Years of Evolving Rivalry in the US Airline Industry
authors: Maria Carballido Cerqueiro, Jesus Carro, Georges Siotis
papers.abstract: This paper aims to better understand competitive rivalry in the US airline industry over the last 25 years. First, it contributes to a better understanding of the procompetitive "Southwest effect" over the period 2000-2025. We show that this effect can clearly be identified during the first part of our sample period, but disappears circa 2016, when Southwest culminated a process of strategic re-orientation and appears to have started behaving like legacy carriers. Second, we find that Southwest presence on a route flattened the relationship between air fares and Multimarket Contact (MMC) until

papers.title: Risk, Specialization, and Covered‐Interest Parity
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Prevailing theories of financial intermediation assume an integrated financial sector with frictionless risk‐sharing. However, we identify substantial risk‐sharing frictions linked to intermediary specialization using currency derivatives markets as a laboratory. Using confidential supervisory data covering $25 trillion in daily bank exposures, we document imperfect hedging in banks' FX‐swap intermediation: banks rarely hedge their synthetic dollar lending with maturity‐matched foreign safe assets. Intermediaries specialize in markets in which they have expertise in managing the assoc

papers.title: Firm Heterogeneity and the Impact of Immigration: Evidence from German Establishments
Buying Data from Consumers: The Impact of Monitoring in U.S. Auto Insurance
The Demand for Mobility: Evidence from an Experiment with Uber Riders
Comment Letters, Connected Investors, and Corporate Bond Issuance
papers.abstract: Using a proprietary data set that documents corporate bond issuances in China, we find that bond regulators’ comment letters (CLs) on issuers’ public disclosures generally target opaque firms and reduce bond issuance success. We also find, however, that connected investors—financial institutions with prior business relationships with the issuers—purchase a relatively larger share of bond issuances from CL recipients than from non-CL recipients, and this greater participation contributes to overpricing. Further analysis shows that connected investors support CL recipients because they possess s

papers.title: DP22038 Personalized Pricing and the Value of Past Purchase Histories: An Empirical Perspective
authors: Isis Durrmeyer, Jean-François Fournel, Mario Samano
papers.abstract: Grocery loyalty programs record purchase histories that retailers do not use to personalize prices. We measure how much they forgo with a structural model of demand and pricing in which a Bayesian seller learns preferences from past purchases and personalizes prices. Profits rise by 7.1\% with one-year histories, capturing two thirds of the gains under perfect knowledge of preferences. Most consumers (84.1\%) gain, but the losses of the minority outweigh these gains, and aggregate consumer surplus falls. An optimal loyalty program charges a membership fee, yet most consumers enroll, because op

papers.title: The Direct and Indirect Effects of Online Job Search Advice
papers.abstract: Abstract We study how online job search advice affects job search behavior and labor market outcomes of unemployed workers. In a large-scale field experiment embedded in the online platform of the Danish public employment service, we provide job seekers with vacancy information and occupational recommendations. Using a two-stage randomized design with regionally varying treatment intensities, we examine both direct effects of advice and treatment spillovers. We find that advice significantly increases employment and earnings when provided to a limited share of job seekers. As treatment intensi

papers.title: The Effect of Small Quasi-Cash Rewards on Prosocial Behavior: The Case of Voluntary Plasma Donations
papers.abstract: To better understand how prosocial behavior can be effectively encouraged, we study four unresolved issues: whether small rewards also motivate prosocial behavior, how short-term effects differ from longer-run behavioral adjustments, whether incentives induce substitution away from other prosocial activities, and whether reminders about existing rewards meaningfully influence behavior. We examine these issues in a long-run randomized field experiment across 12 donation centers of the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders. Donors normally receive one thank-you-coupon (worth €1.5) for a blood donation and

papers.title: DP22037 Dynamic Factor Models and Cointegration
authors: Marco Brianti, Mario Forni, Luca Gambetti, Antonio Granese
papers.abstract: The factors of a stationary Dynamic Factor Model (DFM) are the first differences of singular I(1) processes. Being singular, such processes are always cointegrated. This however does not prevent the existence of a VAR for their first differences, so that the standard estimation procedure of the stationary DFM remains valid. Problems arise only when there is a linear combination of the shocks that has transitory effects on all the variables of the panel. We argue that this case is implausible for macroeconomic data and show that in fact it does not occur for two widely used US data sets — the F

papers.title: DP22036 Beyond Digital Rights: An Institutional Architecture for Consumer Empowerment
authors: Dennis Snower, Paul Twomey, Vicente Arias
papers.abstract: Digital governance has substantially expanded consumers' formal rights over personal data, yet these rights often fail to translate into effective agency in digital markets. We identify this as an institutional capability gap: individual consumers lack the information, expertise, accountability mechanisms, and bargaining capacity required to exercise legal rights continuously and economically effectively. We develop the Innovation in the Digital Economy Architecture (IDEA) as an institutional response. Rather than proposing additional substantive rights, IDEA integrates four mutually reinforci

papers.title: DP22034 Foreign Giants' Broad Shoulders: The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation
authors: Tarek Hassan, Aakash Kalyani, Juan Cruz Lopez Del Valle
papers.abstract: We study the role of foreign ideas in U.S. innovation by constructing a directed “genealogy” of technologies from the full text of 13 million patents filed between 1894 and 2024. By tracing which earlier technologies appear in the founding patents of new ones, we recover a large-scale input–output network of technological recombination that identifies the foreign technologies that serve as inputs into innovation in the United States. We report four main findings. First, foreign ideas are pervasive: 56% ofU.S.technologies build on at least one foreign input, and the most fertile U.S. technologi

papers.title: DP22035 Divisive by Design: Shaping Values in Optimal Mechanisms
papers.abstract: We study a principal who allocates a good to agents with private, independently distributed values through an optimal mechanism. The principal can strategically shape these value distributions by modifying the good’s features, which affect agents’ valuations. Our analysis reveals that optimal designs are frequently divisive – creating goods that appeal strongly to specific agents or agent types while being less valued by others. These divisive designs reduce information rents and increase total surplus, even though they reduce competition. Even when total surplus is constrained, some divisiven

papers.title: DP22033 This Time It's Different: The Role of Women's Employment in Recessions
authors: Titan Alon, Matthias Doepke, Jane Olmstead-Rumsey, James Symons-Hicks, Michèle Tertilt
papers.abstract: We study the transmission of macroeconomic shocks in a model of the household sector featuring single and married households, joint labor-supply decisions of women and men, and childcare needs that interact with the availability of remote work. Recessions concentrated among women are deeper and more persistent than those concentrated among men, reflecting weaker within-family insurance and a new empirical finding that women re-enter employment more slowly after job loss. Yet recovery from the pandemic recession, which had a disproportionate impact on working women due to school closures and th

papers.title: Competing Digital Money
papers.abstract: Abstract We study competition between two payment instruments: bank deposits and digital platform tokens. Using a Hotelling model that integrates the theory of two-sided markets and payment economics, we assess how this competition is affected by a public payment infrastructure that makes private payment instruments interoperable. We show that interoperability, whether implemented as a fast payment system (FPS) or a central bank digital currency (CBDC), may eliminate payment access exclusion and increase trade volumes and social welfare, but at the cost of some disintermediation. When new paym

papers.title: Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets
papers.abstract: Abstract Quality regulation seeks to ensure quality and foster competition by reducing vertical differentiation, but it may also have adverse effects on market structure. We study this trade-off in the context of pharmaceutical bioequivalence, which is the primary quality standard for generic drugs. By exploiting the introduction of bioequivalence in Chile, we find that stronger regulation reduced the number of drugs in the market by 18% and increased average paid prices by 13%. We estimate a model of drug entry, certification, and demand to study how drug quality, aversion to generics, and ce

papers.title: DP22031 Infinite Factor Structure in Conditional Asset Pricing
authors: Mikhail Chernov, Bryan Kelly, Semyon Malamud, Johannes Schwab
papers.abstract: The return covariance matrix is widely assumed to have an eigenvalue cliff: a few large eigenvalues, then a bounded bulk, as in the approximate factor structure of Chamberlain and Rothschild (1983). This premise underlies factor tests, principal-component methods, and large-covariance estimation. These methods estimate moments from returns pooled across states, so they necessarily view a conditional world unconditionally. papers.title: DP22032 Risk Management in Monetary Policy: A Review with Asset Pricing Implications
authors: Anna Cieslak, Stephen Hansen, Hao Pang
papers.abstract: We review recent research on how the Fed's risk-management approach shapes the overall policy stance and how it affects financial market conditions. The evidence shows that the policy stance contains a forward-looking, conditional component that has long been an integral part of the Fed's policymaking toolkit. Asymmetric forward-looking policy tilts — motivated by risk-management considerations and revealed via the Fed's communication — complement and extend beyond the effects of direct policy actions. Drawing on the transcripts of FOMC meetings between 1976 and 2019, we provide an institution

papers.title: The Depositary of Last Resort
papers.abstract: Abstract What are the consequences of making central bank deposits accessible to actors beyond the banking sector? We collect novel micro data on deposit accounts historically held with the Bank of England by individuals and firms other than banks to study their role in the financial panic of 1866. We document that the use of deposit accounts at the central bank soared during the crisis, while commercial banks permanently lost funding. The expansion in the number of active accounts was fueled by individuals, but the intensive margin increase in balances came almost entirely from firms. Recours

papers.title: Collective Activism
papers.abstract: Can investor stewardship codes that call for coordinated activism be satisfied by an Investor Collective Action Organization (ICAO)? In an ICAO, investors work collectively, like a large shareholder, to monitor management and increase value. We analyze the endogenous formation of an ICAO and its equilibrium size, considering free-rider problems and coordination costs. While the ICAO overcomes free-rider problems among its members, it exacerbates them between the ICAO and solo activists. The benefit of joining an ICAO is hump-shaped in size. With moderate coordination costs, ICAO formation feat

papers.title: DP22028 At-Risk or Responsive? Targeting in Unemployment Policy
authors: Sebastian Ernst, Andreas I. Mueller, Johannes Spinnewijn, Joost Bollens
papers.abstract: This paper evaluates the use of algorithmic risk profiling to direct job search support toward individuals most at risk of long-term unemployment. Using three regression discontinuity designs and rich administrative data from the Flemish Public Employment Service (VDAB) in Belgium, we address two key dimensions: whom and when to target. First, job search counseling raises employment on average, but treatment effects decline sharply with predicted risk. This reveals a fundamental trade-off between targeting those most at risk and those most responsive to intervention. Second, we find no evidenc

papers.title: DP22026 Who Can Produce What? Firm Capabilities and Product Entry
authors: Luca Macedoni, John Morrow, Vladimir Tyazhelnikov
papers.abstract: Which firms supply which products? Modeling multi-product firms under heterogeneous markups, we recover firms’ costs for produced products and develop an algorithm inspired by recommender systems to predict costs for unproduced products. Lower predicted costs imply increased product adoption and identify which firms enter when export demand rises, including firms crossing broad product classifications. We use these counterfactual costs to quantify how reductions in fixed and marginal costs induce product entry and lower price indices. In a price-stabilization exercise following a cost shock, e

papers.title: DP22030 Female Jobs and Fertility: Long-term Experimental Evidence from Ethiopian Factories
authors: Andreas Kotsadam, Janneke Pieters, Pauline Rossi, Espen Villanger, Celine Zipfel, Tigabu Getahun
papers.abstract: We conducted an experiment with multiple factories in Ethiopia to test the widespread hypothesis that formal employment among women reduces fertility. Tracking respondents over eight years, we find that women who were randomly offered a job had more children than the control group. The effect on fertility emerged once the effect on wage employment faded away, around three years after baseline. There are clear effects on household income and savings, but not on bargaining power or marriage. papers.title: DP22029 Central Bank Losses and Inflation: 350 Years of Evidence
authors: Anna Grodecka-Messi, Martin Kliem, Gernot Müller
papers.abstract: Are central bank losses inflationary? We show in a simple model that, absent fiscal support, large losses can create a trade-off between stabilizing inflation and stabilizing central bank net worth. We then provide evidence that central bank net worth matters for monetary policy in practice, drawing on a new historical data set with more than 350 years of annual data for Sweden and its central bank, the Riksbank. Using a narrative approach, we identify large adverse shocks to the Riksbank's profitability and trace their dynamic effects. They raise inflation persistently under fiat but not unde

papers.title: DP22021 Valuing Cryptocurrencies: Three Easy Pieces
papers.abstract: Can simple, off-the-shelf models explain positive, persistent, and volatile market valuations of privately issued digital assets? I review ”three easy pieces” - models in which cryptocurrencies can serve as a medium of exchange, a vehicle for saving, and a means of overcoming search and matching frictions in conditional payments. Each functionality imparts positive value, yet interferes with the others. Until these features can be separated, their mutual interference seems likely to inhibit widespread adoption of cryptocurrencies as money.

papers.title: DP22025 Who Benefits from Market Concentration? The Effects of Hospital Mergers on Physician Income.
authors: Jan Boone, Martin Salm, Sofia Santin
papers.abstract: We examine the effect of hospital mergers on the income of medical specialists, with a specific focus on how this effect varies across different contractual arrangements between hospitals and medical specialists. We analyze the effects of 17 mergers that occurred in the Netherlands between 2011 and 2018. Using administrative data and employing a difference-in-differences empirical approach, we find that hospital mergers increase the income of self-employed medical specialists by 3.86\% and do not affect the income of salaried medical specialists. Among the self-employed, mergers lead to signif

papers.title: DP22022 Bayesian Inference for Heteroskedastic Proxy-SVARs
authors: Andrea Carriero, Todd Clark, Massimiliano Marcellino, Tommaso Tornese
papers.abstract: We develop a Bayesian posterior simulation method for SVAR models characterized by conditionally heteroskedastic shocks and nontriangular zero restrictions, a class that includes Proxy-SVARs as a special case. The method embeds a conditional Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) step within a Gibbs sampler. The SMC step exploits an auxiliary homoskedastic model to construct a proposal density and progressively adapts the corresponding particle distribution to incorporate heteroskedasticity, moving through a sequence of intermediate densities. In Monte Carlo experiments, the sampler recovers the structu

papers.title: Generative AI and Firm Values
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT How do recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) affect firm value? We construct the first measure of firms' workforce exposures to Generative AI and show that an “Artificial‐Minus‐Human” portfolio earned 5% in the two weeks following the release of ChatGPT. The labor‐exposure effect is more pronounced for firms with greater data assets and is distinct from the effect of firms' product exposures to AI. We assess whether exposed workforces are substituted or complemented by Generative AI based on whether their exposed tasks are core or supplemental. Examining firms' la

papers.title: The Financial Premium
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We show that bonds issued by financial firms have higher spreads than bonds issued by industrial firms with the same rating and maturity, a difference that we refer to as the financial premium. Over the period 1987 to 2020, in the United States, this premium is 43 basis points on average, with the premium higher for lower ratings, higher during financial crises, and increasing in bond beta. We derive a model that explains the financial premium: banks hold diversified portfolios of nonfinancial debt, and bank debt therefore reflects more systematic risk than nonfinancial debt.

papers.title: Feedback and Contagion through Distressed Competition
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Firms tend to compete more aggressively when facing financial distress. This intensified competition reduces profit margins, pushing them further into distress and adversely affecting their industry peers. To study such feedback and contagion effects, we incorporate strategic competition in a dynamic model with long‐term defaultable debt, exploring various peer interactions such as predation and price wars. papers.title: Predicted Incrementality by Experimentation for Ad Measurement
papers.abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) provide the most credible estimates of advertising incrementality but are difficult to scale. We propose Predicted Incrementality by Experimentation (PIE), which reframes ad measurement as a campaign-level prediction problem. PIE uses a sample of RCTs to learn a mapping from campaign features to causal effects, then applies it to campaigns not run as RCTs. papers.title: When Do Treasuries Earn the Convenience Yield?—A Hedging Perspective
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We document that the convenience yield of U.S. Treasuries exhibits properties consistent with a hedging perspective of safe assets, that is, Treasuries are valued highly if they appreciate with poor aggregate shocks. In particular, the convenience yield tends to be low when the covariance of Treasury returns with the aggregate stock market returns is high. papers.title: Flow‐Driven ESG Returns
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT I show that the recent returns to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) investing are strongly driven by price impact from flows toward ESG portfolios. Using data on trades, I estimate the market's ability to accommodate ESG flows, which is given by the elasticity of substitution between ESG and other stocks. I show that every dollar flowing toward a representative ESG portfolio increases the market value of ESG stocks by $0.8. papers.title: Are Markups Too High? Competition, Strategic Innovation, and Industry Dynamics
papers.abstract: Abstract To study competition, innovation, and industry dynamics that arise as a result of their interaction, we develop a new oligopolistic general-equilibrium Schumpeterian growth model. This model ties together the endogenous growth, oligopolistic competition, and dynamic industrial organization literatures in a single unified framework. Within each industry, there are an endogenously determined number of large firms (“superstars”) that compete á la Cournot and a continuum of small firms which collectively constitute a competitive fringe. Firms dynamically choose their innovation strategies

papers.title: Using Representation Learning and Website Text to Identify Competitor Networks
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a new approach to identify competitors using company websites to map competitive relationships among public and private firms. We apply representation learning techniques to create embeddings of companies based on website content, emphasizing information about industry-specific products and services. By placing all firms, public and private, within the same embedding space, we construct a peer competitor network that supports analysis of company interactions and market evolution. We label this new approach and set of network competitors as the website text-based network i

papers.title: Personalization, Engagement, and Content Quality on Social Media: An Evaluation of Reddit’s News Feed
papers.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly curate their content through personalized algorithmic feeds. Platforms have an incentive to promote content that increases the predicted engagement of each user to lift advertising revenues. This paper studies how ranking content to maximize engagement affects the credibility of news content with which users engage. In addition, I evaluate how the ranking algorithm itself can be designed to promote engagement with high-credibility content. Using data from the Reddit politics community, I exploit a novel discontinuity in the ranking algorithm to identify the causa

papers.title: Directing the Labor Market: Shared Directors and Employee Flows
papers.abstract: Abstract Using résumé data on over 20 million U.S. workers, we find that the flow of employees between a pair of firms sharply drops by about 20% during periods in which the firms share a board director. This relationship is stronger in settings where firms have greater potential gains from limiting worker mobility and is most pronounced for higher-skilled employees. Moreover, we find more connected firms have lower rates of internal promotion and no improvements in employee satisfaction. The evidence is consistent with shared directors serving as a mechanism for labor market coordination.

papers.title: Central Bank Economic Transparency and Managerial Learning
papers.abstract: Abstract Central banks increasingly disclose their private information regarding the economy’s current and future state (CBET). Consistent with CBET shifting investors’ collection and pricing of aggregate-level (where managers do not have an information advantage) toward firm-level (where managers do have an information advantage) information, we find that CBET reduces managers’ learning from stock price. papers.title: The Marginal Propensity to Hire
papers.abstract: Abstract When financial constraints bind, firms adjust employment in response to cash flow shocks. A 2010 revaluation of business rates, a UK tax levied on business-occupied properties, implied that similar firms, occupying similar properties in narrow geographical locations, experienced different tax changes. I find that, on average, for every ￡1 of additional cash flow triggered by the tax change, 39 pence were spent on employment, with small and leveraged firms responding the most. I use these findings to discipline a general equilibrium model with firm heterogeneity and financial frictions

papers.title: Trading Off Business and Family Investments: Evidence from U.S. Entrepreneurial Households
papers.abstract: Investing in children’s human capital reduces business investments for U.S. entrepreneurial households. Using financial account data of 90,000 small businesses linked to their owners and a regression discontinuity design that compares the business performance of households with college-aged dependents (18–22) to those with near-college-aged dependents (14–17), I show that business revenues and expenses decline sharply when owners’ children reach age 18. Despite the declines, profitability and productivity remain largely unaffected, suggesting a general downsizing rather than a loss in efficien

papers.title: Money Creation for Crypto Space: Stablecoins or Central Bank Digital Currencies?
papers.abstract: Stablecoins are the current go-to digital money to settle transactions on the blockchain. We explore the implications of introducing competing tokenized public digital monies (i.e., tokenized central bank digital currencies (CBDCs)). When they pay a moderate interest rate and guarantee users’ anonymity, tokenized CBDCs crowd out stablecoins. However, when they pay a high interest rate and have low anonymity features, stablecoin issuers could use tokenized CBDCs as collateral, promoting the creation of stablecoins. We identify conditions under which introducing a CBDC to compete with stablecoin

papers.title: Creation After Destruction? Financial Intermediation and Firm Entry After Bank Cleanups
papers.abstract: Abstract We study a large and unanticipated bank cleanup in India after prolonged zombie lending under regulatory forbearance. The cleanup forced widespread zombie exits through bankruptcy. In contrast to a frictionless world where entry automatically follows exit, we show that with financial frictions, local banking conditions shape creation after destruction. papers.title: The Welfare Effects of Selling Leads in a Two-Sided Marketplace
papers.abstract: Digital platforms that connect customers with service providers often monetize by selling customer leads to interested providers. Examples include Bark, Google Local Services, HomeAdvisor, Modernize, Porch, and Thumbtack. This paper develops a game-theoretic model to analyze how lead pricing affects customer and provider welfare. papers.title: A Model of the Attention Economy: Data, Platforms, and Discovery
papers.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic model of the attention economy featuring two interlinked markets: a product market, where consumers have limited awareness of firms, and an attention market, where platforms attract attention by investing in free services (e.g., social media, streaming, podcasts) and sell targeted ads using data on consumer preferences. papers.title: Taxing Top Wealth: Migration Responses and Their Aggregate Economic Implications
papers.abstract: Using administrative data from Scandinavian countries, we provide evidence on international migration responses to wealth taxes and evaluate their aggregate economic implications. We find significant migration responses among the wealthy: A 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate decreases the stock of wealthy taxpayers by about 2 percent. papers.abstract: Americans rarely marry outside their race or class group, a pattern with well-documented implications for inequality and intergenerational mobility. Limited exposure may partly explain these low intergroup marriage rates. We instrument for exposure using variation in childhood neighborhoods based on whether other race and class groups had more opposite-sex children of similar age. papers.abstract: We study racial disparities in promotions in a setting in which promotions are formulaic: the US patent office. Using detailed administrative data that allow us to observe who is eligible for promotion when, we document that Black patent examiners experience delays in promotions they are entitled to, slowing their climb to the top of the career ladder by a year and reducing career earnings by 2.5 percent. papers.title: Fighting for Growth: Labor Scarcity and Technological Progress during the British Industrial Revolution
papers.abstract: We establish a link between labor scarcity and the adoption of laborsaving technology in industrializing England. During the Napoleonic Wars, more than 10 percent of the male population served in the armed forces. Where recruitment was heavy, more machines economizing on labor were adopted. Naval recruitment, instrumented by warships' coastal access, provides exogenous variation in labor scarcity and suggests that the link between labor shortages and adoption is causal. Knowledge Spillovers, Competition, and Individual Careers
papers.abstract: Exposure to better peers in the workplace can influence career trajectories through two opposing channels: positively, via knowledge spillovers, and negatively, through competition for advancement. papers.abstract: A principal decides which party deserves a prize. Only the parties observe the state that determines who is deserving. The principal gives each party a text describing the conditions under which that party deserves the prize and asks each to report the state. The parties are nonstrategic. papers.abstract: What are the implications of unequal access to innovation careers for the direction of innovation and inequality? Leveraging novel linked datasets in the United States and Finland, we document that innovators create products more likely to be purchased by consumers like them in terms of gender, socioeconomic status, and age. papers.abstract: We analyze consumer surplus when a monopolist can adjust both prices and product qualities across segments, engaging in secondand third-degree price discrimination simultaneously. We characterize the consumer-optimal segmentation and show that it has a striking structure: Consumers with the same value receive the same quality in every segment, though prices differ. papers.title: Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty
papers.abstract: Abstract People may fail to recall and use information they already know when making decisions. We empirically investigate whether such “retrieval failures” distort consumption-smoothing behavior among Zambian farmers, who derive their income from one annual harvest and spend it over the course of the year. We document that individuals underestimate upcoming spending by 50%, creating scope for undersaving. papers.abstract: We study contemporaneous and post-program impacts of a public works program which provides urban youth seven months of employment at the formal minimum wage with complementary training in entrepreneurship or job search. papers.title: Detection of Collusive Networks in Multistage Auctions
papers.abstract: We develop a method for detecting cartels in multistage auctions. Our approach allows firms to act collusively against cartel members yet competitively otherwise. papers.title: Innovation through Inventor Mobility: Evidence from Noncompete Agreements
papers.abstract: Proponents of labor mobility restrictions argue that innovation incentives more than offset harm to workers. Yet the causal effect of such policies on innovation is an open empirical question. Leveraging plausibly exogenous state-level changes in the enforceability of noncompete agreements (NCAs), we find a significant negative effect on innovation. papers.abstract: Using itinerary-level global air traffic data, this paper proposes a novel instrumental variable to estimate the effect of in-person interactions on bilateral trade. By exploiting exogenous variations in air connectivity that are driven by third-country connecting capacities, we show that increased air connections boost trade, especially for complex industries and new products. papers.abstract: We conduct survey experiments to test how the design of scientific grants—the money and time awarded—can be used to manage researchers. On average, researchers are relatively unwilling to trade off money for time when choosing among grants. However, there is significant heterogeneity in researchers' preferences. papers.title: Disastrous Displacement: The Long-Run Impacts of Landslides
papers.abstract: Natural disasters displace millions of people a year, but their economic impacts are difficult to study when the affected population becomes dispersed. This paper estimates the long-run impacts of six landslides in Uganda on nearly the full affected population. papers.abstract: We analyze mandatory retirement in Sweden, which eliminates employment protection at age 67. papers.title: University as a Melting Pot: Long-Term Effects of Internationalization
papers.abstract: This paper provides the first evidence on the impact of exposure to international students on the long-term outcomes of native students. I combine unique survey and administrative data from the Netherlands covering one million students across three decades and employ an across-cohort design. papers.title: Who Gets a Family? The Consequences of Family and Congregate Care Allocation for Child Outcomes
papers.abstract: Hundreds of thousands of children grow up in the US foster care system every year and are at high risk of experiencing negative outcomes such as incarceration and homelessness. This paper documents how the placement of foster children into families rather than congregate care improves their outcomes, using the exits of other children from families as an instrument for their placement setting. papers.title: Globalization, Capital Taxation, and Development: Evidence from a Macrohistorical Database
papers.abstract: This paper builds and analyzes a new global macrohistorical database of effective tax rates on capital and labor in 154 countries. We establish a new stylized fact: While effective capital tax rates fell in developed countries between 1965 and 2018, they rose in developing countries after 1990. papers.title: Early Grade Retention Harms Adult Earnings
papers.abstract: This paper provides new causal evidence on the effects of grade retention on educational attainment, behavioral outcomes, and labor market performance by analyzing Texas's reading test–based retention policy. Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, I find that third-grade retention significantly reduces annual earnings at age 26 by $3,477 (19 percent). papers.title: The Long-Term Effects of Cash Assistance
papers.abstract: We investigate the long-term effects of cash assistance on beneficiaries and their children among participants in the Seattle-Denver Income Maintenance Experiment. Treated families in this randomized experiment received thousands of dollars in extra government benefits for three or five years in the 1970s. papers.abstract: Many people are impatient. We introduce domain-specific discounting to a contracting model and test a strategy for improving incentives when people are impatient over effort: implement time-bundled contracts that make the payment for future effort increase in current effort. Using a randomized evaluation of an exercise incentive program among diabetics in India, we find that time-bundled contracts generate equivalent effort to time-separable contracts at 15 percent lower cost. papers.title: Oil Prices, Monetary Policy, and Inflation Surges
papers.abstract: We develop a simple quantitative New Keynesian model aimed at analyzing how the reaction of monetary policy contributed to the recent rise and fall in inflation. papers.title: Leaning against the Global Financial Cycle
papers.abstract: We investigate the impact of institutional quality on shielding emerging economies from the global financial cycle. Our findings indicate that countries with a higher rule of law, characterized by superior contract enforcement and more robust protection of property rights, experience a less severe tightening of domestic financial and macroeconomic conditions when faced with adverse global financial shocks. papers.abstract: In less developed economies, the allocation of factor inputs to more productive farms is often hindered. To analyze how distortions affect farm dynamics and agricultural productivity, we develop a model of heterogeneous farms investing in productivity improvements. papers.abstract: Economic growth is typically measured in per capita terms. A long tradition in philosophy, however, suggests that social welfare may depend on the number of people as well. papers.abstract: This study analyzes how firms form their inflation expectations after a regime change in monetary policy and a transition to a low-inflation environment. papers.abstract: The US health-services sector has grown in terms of its expenditure share and relative price. Using a two-sector general equilibrium model with monopolistic competition and endogenous population, we find that relative price growth is almost entirely attributable to increasing relative sectoral markups. papers.abstract: We develop a model of the joint behavior of optimal tax rates and government spending over the business cycle to explain procyclical fiscal policy in emerging markets. papers.abstract: Do changes in aggregate volatility alter the impulse response of output to monetary policy? papers.abstract: We study how firm heterogeneity and market power affect macroeconomic fragility, defined as the probability of long slumps. papers.abstract: We address the joint assortment and inventory optimization problem for an online retailer facing a set of N substitutable products.
